Q: How can I kill a process running on particular port in Linux? A:

To build on what @veer7 said:

If you want to know what was on the port, do this before you kill it.

$ sudo netstat -plten |grep java
tcp6       0      0 127.0.0.1:8005          :::*                    LISTEN      1000       906726      25296/java
tcp6       0      0 :::8009                 :::*                    LISTEN      1000       907503      25296/java
tcp6       0      0 :::8080                 :::*                    LISTEN      1000       907499      25296/java

$ ps 25296
  PID TTY      STAT   TIME COMMAND
25296 ?        Sl     0:16 /usr/lib/jvm/java-8-openjdk-amd64/bin/java -Dcatalina.base=/hom

Use 'ps' and the number of the processes that netstat reported back.

Q: Why am I getting different results when extracting intermediate variables from Scipy solve_ivp ODE function? A:

The behavior you're seeing is expected and comes from how solve_ivp works internally, not necessarily from an error in your model.

The key point is that solve_ivp does not evaluate your ODE only at the accepted time steps (results.t). It uses an adaptive method, so your function is called many times at intermediate points (and even for rejected steps).

Because of that, when you store values like this:
self.plasmid_transfer_val.update({t: plasmid_transfer})

you are collecting values from all internal solver evaluations, not just the final accepted solution points. These t values will not match results.t exactly (due to floating-point differences and rejected steps), which explains why filtering them later gives inconsistent or incorrect results.

Why your approaches differ

1. Storing inside the ODE function

  • Includes intermediate and rejected steps

  • t values don’t align exactly with results.t

  • Same time may be evaluated multiple times

So this data cannot be reliably matched to the final solution.

2. Recomputing afterward

This is the correct approach, but it must be done properly. Your function expects a single state vector, while results.y is a 2D array.

You should compute it like this:

plasmid_transfer = [
    ode_lotka.simple_plasmid(model.results.y[:, i], conjugation_rate)
    for i in range(len(model.results.t))
]

This ensures that:

  • You use only accepted solution points

  • The values are consistent with results.y

  • No floating-point matching issues occur

    About the “incorrect” values

    Seeing plasmid_transfer larger than X[2] is not necessarily wrong. The expression

    X[1] * (conjugation_rate * (X[0] + X[2]))

    represents a rate, not a population, so it can exceed the size of a single compartment.

    Also note that this line in your code:

    self.dTdt.update({t: X[2] + dTdt})

    is not comparable to results.y[2], because dTdt is a derivative. You would need to integrate it over time (i.e., multiply by a time step) to compare it to state values.

Recommended approach

The most reliable solution is:

Solve the system first, then compute any intermediate quantities from results.y.

Avoid storing intermediate values inside the ODE function unless you explicitly handle solver internals.

Q: How can I center align only one author amongst three other authors in LaTeX? A:

Just to add clarity to samcarter-is-at-topanswers-xyz's answer, the fix proposed by Werner, which I confirm works, is as follows.

Step 1: right before \begin{document}, add:

\makeatletter
\newcommand{\linebreakand}{%
  \end{@IEEEauthorhalign}
  \hfill\mbox{}\par
  \mbox{}\hfill\begin{@IEEEauthorhalign}
}
\makeatother

Step 2: in the author list, before the author that is on the new line, replace the \and by \linebreakand.

Example: PDF, image, LaTeX sources.

Q: Some coding issues A:

A principal strategy for problem solving is breaking down a bigger problem into smaller ones. If a system seems daunting, you may be failing to grasp the "big picture", i.e. the translatable steps between the original "problem" (e.g. your large system) and the smaller subproblems it is broken into. You break the big problem into smaller ones, which in turn are broken into even smaller problems, until the problems are trivial to solve.

Q: Why would anyone use VCL when there is FMX? A:

The much larger and more varied third party ecosystem for VCL is another reason. It's improved for FMX since the early years but there's a lot more gaps in the available third party controls than there is for VCL.

Don't get me wrong. I like FMX (mostly, the styling engine is the worst part) and I use it whenever I can to keep my cross platform options open.

If I'm writing software that needs a sophisticated user interface though and I know supporting Windows is all that will ever be needed, VCL is easier to write and produces a more polished result.

Q: Does an alias table need a primary key? Is the key just a composite of all the columns? A:

Thanks but, while I know that making a primary key using both columns is considered best practice, I'm just not sure why.

For my other tables, I can see the primary key helps with joins or quick lookups. But for this use case, it does not. It will never be joined on this composite (2-column) key, and all queries will be based on just one column (gameid). So what does the primary key actually help with in this use case..?
